paras: The attempted lynching of Emanuel Gaskin took place in Kershaw County, South Carolina, near Camden, in December 1888, when a crowd tried to lynch Gaskin, a Black man accused of murdering a woman named Betsy Clark. Gaskin was hurried away to jail, and one account credits the sheriff and his deputies with rescuing him. Northern papers carried the story chiefly for the alleged murder, reporting the lynching attempt in a closing sentence.

According to a dispatch dated December 9, Clark met Gaskin, described as "colored," on a lonely road in Kershaw County on the morning of December 8. The Sun's version said he insulted her and attempted to assault her, then stabbed her and severed her head. The Connecticut Western News, which spelled the names "Bessie Clark" and "Gaskins," reported the stabbing and beheading near Camden but did not mention an assault.

Once the body was found, by a party of sportsmen according to the Connecticut paper, a search was organized, and Gaskin joined it. The Sun said a white man noticed his excitement and charged him with the crime, while the Connecticut paper said a member of the party saw a spot of blood on his sleeve. Both reports said that after first denying the charge he confessed when taken before a Trial Justice or magistrate.

A crowd then moved to lynch him; the Sun described it as "principally negroes" and said Gaskin "was hurried away to jail." In the Connecticut account the sheriff and his deputies rescued him and lodged him in jail at Camden.
No report of an inquest, trial or later outcome for Gaskin appears in the coverage.

The New York Sun ran the dispatch on December 10 under the headline "DIED TO SAVE HER HONOR. A Woman Killed by a Negro who Met her on a Lonely Road," framing the story around the alleged assault. Two days later the Connecticut Western News printed a shorter item headed "A Cool Murderer," stressing the accused's calm after the killing. Neither paper commented on the crowd, treating the averted lynching as a coda to the murder story.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Emanuel Gaskin
bases: A crowd was about to lynch, or attempted to lynch, a Black man accused of murder, and he was taken to jail unharmed (A1, A2).

Both reports say a crowd tried or was about to lynch Gaskin over the alleged murder, but he was hurried away or rescued and lodged in jail, so no one was killed by the crowd (A1, A2); the crowd's size is not given.

Two reports with different wording and details (Kershaw county vs. near Camden; a white man vs. a member of a party of sportsmen as accuser; Sheriff and deputies named only in A2) agree on the murder accusation, confession, attempted lynching and jailing (A1, A2).

accounts.label: New York Sun dispatch
accounts.gist: Gaskin insulted and tried to assault Clark, stabbed her and severed her head; a white man accused him during the search; he confessed before a Trial Justice; a crowd, mostly Black, was about to lynch him but he was hurried to jail.

accounts.label: Connecticut Western News item
accounts.gist: Gaskins stabbed Bessie Clark near Camden and severed her head; sportsmen found the body; a searcher saw blood on his sleeve; he confessed before a magistrate; the crowd attempted to lynch him and the Sheriff and deputies rescued him.

framing.detail: The Sun's headline 'DIED TO SAVE HER HONOR' framed the story around the alleged assault and murder; the averted lynching is reported in one closing sentence without comment.
Headlined 'A Cool Murderer,' the Connecticut item stressed the accused's composure and reported the rescue by the Sheriff without comment on the crowd.

info: The killing of Clark was reported as occurring on the morning of Dec. 8, 1888 ('yesterday morning' in a Dec. 9 dispatch); the lynching attempt followed the search and hearing, date not stated separately.
A lonely road in Kershaw county (A1); near Camden, S. C. (A2). A1's dispatch is datelined 'COLUMBUS, S. C.'

Target of the lynching attempt: Emanuel Gaskin (A1) or Gaskins (A2), described as 'colored' and 'a negro'. Betsy (A1) or Bessie (A2) Clark was the murder victim in the alleged crime, not a target of the crowd.
Accused of stabbing Clark and severing her head; A1 adds that he insulted her and attempted to assault her. Both say he confessed before a Trial Justice or magistrate.
Gaskin was hurried away to jail (A1) / rescued by the Sheriff and deputies and lodged in jail at Camden (A2). No report of a trial or later outcome was found.

sources.note: Dispatch datelined 'COLUMBUS, S. C., Dec. 9': Gaskin accused of killing Betsy Clark in Kershaw county; confessed before a Trial Justice; crowd 'principally negroes' about to lynch him; hurried to jail.
quotes: The crowd, principally negroes, was about to lynch Gaskin, but he was hurried away to jail.
He was taken before a Trial Justice, where blood was found on his clothing, and he confessed the whole thing.
